paper_metadata.title: High-temperature strength of titanium alloys alloyed with silicon, aluminum, and zirconium in air

evidence.quote: We study the behavior of VT1-0 titanium alloy alloyed with silicon, aluminum, and zirconium in the process of oxidation in air at 800°C for 30 h.
The alloys were prepared by using the procedure of plasma skull melting.
The alloy was additionally alloyed with silicon (1–6 wt.%), aluminum (3 wt.%), and zirconium (5 wt.%). Cast specimens were not subjected to thermal treatment for oxidation.

The alloys were prepared by using the procedure of plasma skull melting. The temperature of a casting mold was equal to 1700°C and the pressure in the melting chamber varied within the range 0.1–0.6 MPa. The temperature of the molten metal and its chemical composition were equalized by electromagnetic stirring.

Specimens 10 × 4 × 3 mm in size were oxidized in a “Derivatograph” device (the changes in the mass were continuously recorded for 6 h) and in a resistance furnace at 800°C [the mass was periodically measured for the entire period of holding (up to 30 h)].
In all cases, the X-ray phase diffraction analysis shows that scale is mainly formed by the Ti O2 phase (ru- tile).
Moreover, the traces of silicon dioxide ( α-Si O2 ) and aluminum oxide ( γ-Al2 O3 ) are also detected in al- loys.
Moreover, the traces of silicon dioxide ( α-Si O2 ) and aluminum oxide ( γ-Al2 O3 ) are also detected in al- loys.

As a result of alloying of VT1-0 alloy with silicon in amounts greater than  0.45 wt.%, we observe the formation of silicides in its structure. These silicides precipitate on grain boundaries and in side the grains decelerating the diffusion of titanium and oxygen ions and, hence, the formation of titanium dioxide.
In the alloys additionally alloyed w ith aluminum, we observe the formation of complex-alloy silicides (Ti, Zr)5 (Al, Si) 3 .
In the unalloyed material, the multilayer scale begins to crumble after testing for 10 h (Fig. 2a). Its structure is fine-grained and homogeneous (Fig. 3a).
The cracks are located in the outer layer (Fig. 3b).
In alloys with 2–6% of silicon, the layer of scale contains elongated crystals whose number increases if we introduce 3% of aluminum.

After a certain period of time, we observe the formation of cavities on the scale–metal interface, which turn into barriers for the transition of ions into scale as the temperature and duration of holding increase.

The microhardness of the surface layers and the base metal of alloys and the depth of saturation show that the metal layer neighboring with the layer of scale is characterized by elevated hardness (Table 3, Fig. 2b), which gradually decreases with depth (Fig. 2b).

In the alloys containing silicon, the dissolution of this element in titanium (the maximum solubility of silicon in α-titanium is 0.45 wt.% at a temperature of the eutectoid transformation equal to 860˚C) decreases the lattice constant of the latter and inhibits diffusion.

mechanisms.name: silicide precipitation barrier to Ti and O diffusion

evidence.quote: These silicides precipitate on grain boundaries and in side the grains decelerating the diffusion of titanium and oxygen ions and, hence, the formation of titanium dioxide.

The data of metallographic analysis, together with the data on microhardness, show that, in the process of oxidation of titanium, oxygen dissolves in the surface layer of the metal parallel with the formation of an oxide film.

mechanisms.name: alloying change of scale morphology improving adhesion

evidence.quote: However, under the influence of alloying, the structural morphology changes and the level of adhesion increases, which significantly decreases the rate of oxidation.

mechanisms.name: dissolution of Al and Zr in TiO2 lattice loosening scale

evidence.quote: The amounts of formed aluminum and zirconium oxides are very small but the dissolution of these elements in the Ti O2 lattice promotes its loosening and, hence, the process of diffusion of oxygen through titanium dioxide is accelerated [5].

mechanisms.name: impaired lattice diffusion by Al and Zr solutes
